5'9", 155lbs checking in. My mile PB is 5:15, and I've run a 18:12 5k and 1:23 half.

Train well, eat well and healthily and you'll get there.

Also, and I know it isn't quite this easy, try to stop comparing yourself to other runners. Fitness is a journey, we're all starting from different places.

Keep well, friend.

Also in this position, potentially DNSing in a couple of weeks.

Just explain that you were injured and running the marathon would have done a lot more damage and it was a sensible decision not to run. Own the decision, because it's the right one.
I hang mine up so they air, and accept that they're going to smell a little when I leave...
Not OP, but just observing that every time I see you pop up you're full of excellent advice and wanted to say thanks :)

Personally, I don't drink during anything shorter than a half; you may find you need to drink on a shorter run, but the only way to find out is by experimenting. I'd also suggest trying out running outdoors - things like heat indoors vs weather outdoors may make a huge difference to your thirst.

Find out if the race has cups or bottles, or even if it's cupless (ie bring your own). It's unlikely for a race of that distance, but possible. Practise drinking out of them before you get there and find a strategy that works for you. Personally, I can't drink out of cups on the run, so in that case I'll walk all the water stations. 10 paces or so at walking pace won't break your rhythm. Alternatively, if you're more comfortable bringing a bottle, then do that! It's your race, after all :)

I'm a week out from my marathon and sidelined by shin splints. I've done no running for a week and lots of RICEing.

At this point I'm entirely open to DNSing or a tactical DNF; I don't want to be out for an extended period.

On the bright side, it's feeling much better today than it did yesterday even, so there's hope yet!

Any pro tips on getting better?

>So im thinking of running 6 or 7 miles at my target HM pace - because, in all honesty, I really dont know how it 'feels'!

Have you got a recent benchmark to go from? I'd go and do the 10k TT; I remember doing that one in Edinburgh when I was following that plan. It's tough, but a massive confidence boost when you pull it off! Go and do four laps of East Park, I believe in you!

Enjoy takeaway, and happy birthday to wee man!

> probably going to pace around a clubmate instead

Lucky socks are nothing but a placebo / the key to success\*

Good luck!
I don't remember having any issues there; just beware of cars on the stretch by the old police station. Also, I'm not a fan of running too many laps!

I've just picked up a Vivoactive 3 off ebay and been pleasantly surprised. It looks great, it's smaller than my other watch and does all of the sports. The only downsides are that some of the data fields are somewhat limited with what you can put on them, and the battery life is obviously a lot shorter.
If you don't want to run, or you feel it isn't safe, you have every right not to turn up regardless of if it goes ahead or not. Look after number 1.

If I only take a couple of walking breaks, it's still a run. If I'm doing something structured like what you describe, I'd call it run/walking. Regardless, distance covered is distance covered.

As to getting back to running the full distance, it sounds like you're going the right way about it. If anything, slow the running intervals down - you don't want to be pushing hard while your knees recover.

TBH neither did I - I had a quick look on eBay for a stand-by while my fenix was off being repaired - no lap button means it's not great for a track session but you can load up preprogrammed intervals just fine, if anything it's better at swimming than the fenix and links with all the sensors etc on my turbo bike.

I've also used it for a race and loaded up "race screen" just fine which had all the data I could've asked for :)

First of all, you shouldn't always be giving your max. You should be aiming for around 80% easy running and maybe 20% hard, or one run a week hard if your mileage isn't massive.

Second, build up slowly. Find a route/parkrun you can time yourself over or make yourself a strava segment so you can track progress. Once every few weeks, give it more effort over your route and see yourself progress - you'll find the limit sooner or later :)
u/shaebay is correct, however as a starting point I would definitely cut back mileage or rest up and allow yourself to recover. I'd like to reiterate though, please go and talk to your doctor.
I like a beer the night before a marathon - you'll be fine!

Consistency is key - you should aim to run your intervals at a speed you can maintain for the session. For example, if you're running 12 x 400 in 90s, you should be aiming to cover *every* 400 in 90 seconds. Likewise, if you're doing it by time, aim to cover the same distance in your 2-minute intervals every time.

Pacing practice is important - it's important to be able to gauge your effort levels so that you can complete the session.

I can't answer about the shoes - however, if this is going to become a regular thing I'd go to your local running shop and try out a few pairs to make sure they're comfortable.

As for C25K, the key things are to take the run segments slow, like slower than you think slow, and respect your rest days. There's an excellent community over at r/c25k who know the program inside out. Good luck!
Hard to say without more info, but I'd also suggest seeing a physio.
Go to your local running shop and try a few on the treadmill - don't get too hung up on brands/models and find a shoe that works for you.
If they've done something special, yes. If they've just done an easy jog, not so much.

Nope. Nonononono. No.

Mostly because you're likely to damage your knee - I'd check with the doc if you're OK to run on it at all tbh.
I'd recommend going to see a physio - they'll be able to tell you exactly what's wrong and give you exercises to do to get you back up and running.

Ultimately - don't overdo it. The hay is in the barn, you won't get any real benefit from extra mileage at this point - it's more important to let it recover.

I'd recommend taking the rest of the week off; if you're really desperate go for a test run on Saturday or Sunday and see how it feels, and let that inform your next week of taper.

You won't lose any real fitness from a week out, and the priority is letting the ankle heal.

Congratulations - that's hella fast! I'd recommend you make a training post in r/artc \- they're very good at helping out with these advanced training questions if you follow the posting format and give them a lot of information to work with.

As far as the basics go, upping mileage, running mostly easy, throw in some interval/tempo work and see where you go.

I'm a fan of Pfitzinger's plans from Advanced Marathoning - it's worth picking up the book and finding a plan that works for you. Other coaches are available (Hanson, Daniels etc...)

I use race screen too and it's great until the GPS gets out of sync - I ran the Big Half in London using it and gps went screwy around Canary Wharf (as you would expect), but it was so far out it corrected up a mile rather than down. I just switched to running by HR (the coloured number on the screen is dead handy!) and came in not *too* far off goal time.

Did me proud in Paris on Sunday and I use it for club races etc too and I think it's brilliant (most of the time).

NB test it out a couple of times before your big race.

tagging u/ravenx92 for visibility.

Stop overthinking it, you'll be fine.

If you want to wear shorts (race day or any other time) wear the damn shorts, no-one's judging you!

That said - nothing new on race day. You might find you get some rubbing that you don't with tights, so definitely worth doing a couple of test runs with them and be prepared to get hold of some vaseline/bodyglide.
